context:
Journey stage L4 (2027-07-07), same patient later in the disease course.
INTERVAL HISTORY: WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED (2027-05-12 to 2027-07-07)

- Referred to the cellular therapy center. Leukapheresis 2027-05-27. Bridging: dexamethasone pulse and
  radiotherapy to the retroperitoneal mass (20 Gy in 5 fractions).
- Lymphodepletion fludarabine/cyclophosphamide 2027-06-26 to 06-28.
- Axicabtagene ciloleucel infused 2027-07-01 (day 0).
- Day 2: fever 38.6 C, normotensive, no oxygen (CRS grade 1). Day 3: tocilizumab 8 mg/kg x1; fever resolved.
- Prophylaxis: levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily since day 0, acyclovir, fluconazole. Atovaquone for
  Pneumocystis prophylaxis is planned (sulfonamide allergy).

RAPID RESPONSE NOTE, DAY +6 (2027-07-07, 06:40), cellular therapy unit

Overnight the nurse noted new confusion. This morning he reports a severe headache and has vomited twice.
His wife says he could not find words for objects last night and his handwriting "looks strange".

Vitals: T 38.9 C, HR 112, BP 96/58 (baseline 124/76), RR 22, SpO2 95% on room air.
Neuro: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6). Oriented to person only. ICE score 2/10 (not oriented to year, month, city or
hospital; names 1 of 3 objects; follows commands; cannot write a standard sentence; cannot count backwards
from 100 by 10). No focal limb weakness. Pupils equal and
reactive. No neck stiffness. No witnessed seizure activity. Mild tremor of both hands.
Chest clear. Abdomen soft. Central line site clean.

Current medications: levetiracetam 500 mg BID, acyclovir 400 mg BID, fluconazole 400 mg daily,
insulin correction scale, ondansetron PRN, pantoprazole.

Labs 05:30:
  WBC 0.4 x10^3/uL (ANC 0.2), Hb 8.6 g/dL, platelets 44 x10^3/uL
  Na 131 mmol/L, K 3.6, creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, glucose 242 mg/dL
  CRP 214 mg/L (<5), ferritin 4,820 ng/mL (30-400)
  INR 1.3, fibrinogen 210 mg/dL (200-400)
  Lactate 2.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.0)

Questions: What do you consider first (immediate priorities)? | What are your differential diagnoses? | How do you investigate?

answer.q1: Immediate priorities: recognize grade 3 ICANS (ICE 2/10, GCS 13, new confusion, severe headache, vomiting, word-finding and handwriting difficulty, tremor) with concurrent CRS (fever, hypotension) and possible neutropenic sepsis, and manage all three simultaneously in an ICU or step-down setting. First, ABCs and hemodynamics: oxygen, continuous monitoring, two large-bore IVs, an isotonic crystalloid bolus of 500-1000 mL for BP 96/58, then norepinephrine to maintain MAP at least 65 mmHg if fluid-refractory; avoid hypotonic fluids and avoid fluid overload because of possible cerebral edema. Second, obtain blood cultures and start broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour (piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime, adding vancomycin for central-line/MRSA risk) because ANC 0.2, fever and lactate 2.6 make sepsis the most dangerous reversible cause. Third, treat ICANS immediately with dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours; if there is no improvement within 24 hours, or if he develops grade 4 ICANS or cerebral edema, escalate to methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3 days and add mannitol or hypertonic saline with neurosurgical input. Fourth, give a repeat tocilizumab 8 mg/kg IV for the CRS component; tocilizumab does not cross the blood-brain barrier and does not treat ICANS itself. Fifth, increase levetiracetam to 750-1000 mg twice daily (renally adjusted), obtain an urgent EEG, and treat clinical seizures with benzodiazepines. Sixth, obtain an emergent noncontrast CT head to exclude hemorrhage and edema, followed by MRI brain with contrast and MRV; defer lumbar puncture until imaging is reviewed and platelets/coagulation are corrected. Seventh, evaluate and treat for HLH/MAS and TMA and cover CNS infection. Finally, transfuse platelets to at least 50,000/uL before procedures, manage glucose and sodium carefully, and involve critical care, neurology, cellular therapy and pharmacy. Do not delay antibiotics or steroids for imaging or lumbar puncture.
answer.q2: The differential is led by ICANS, grade 3, possibly with cerebral edema and concurrent CRS, because of the timing (day +6 after axicabtagene ciloleucel), the ICE score of 2/10, headache, vomiting, word-finding difficulty, handwriting change and tremor. I must simultaneously exclude neutropenic sepsis with septic encephalopathy: ANC 0.2, central line, fever, relative hypotension, lactate 2.6 and CRP 214 make infection the most urgent alternative. CNS infection is a major concern, including HSV encephalitis, VZV, CMV, EBV, HHV-6 (a classic post-CAR-T limbic encephalitis associated with confusion, seizures and hyponatremia), JC/PML, bacterial meningitis, and fungal infection such as aspergillus or cryptococcus; acyclovir 400 mg twice daily may not prevent breakthrough. CAR-T-associated HLH/MAS (IEC-HS) is also likely given ferritin 4820, cytopenias, fever, coagulopathy, and possible liver dysfunction. Other considerations are nonconvulsive status epilepticus, intracerebral hemorrhage, ischemic stroke, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (headache and vomiting with platelets 44 and INR 1.3), PRES (less likely with low blood pressure but possible with endothelial injury), thrombotic microangiopathy, and metabolic or toxic encephalopathy from hyponatremia 131, hyperglycemia 242, hypoxia, uremia, or medications such as acyclovir, levetiracetam and ondansetron. I would also keep CNS lymphoma progression in mind given his high CNS-IPI, though the acute day +6 timing strongly favors ICANS; adrenal insufficiency from prior adrenal involvement and drug fever are lower-probability considerations. The key is to treat ICANS and sepsis simultaneously while excluding CNS infection and HLH.
answer.q3: Investigations should proceed in parallel with treatment. Blood: two sets of blood cultures from peripheral sites and each central-line lumen, urine culture, sputum culture and chest radiograph, lactate and arterial blood gas, CBC with peripheral smear for schistocytes, comprehensive metabolic panel and liver tests, coagulation, fibrinogen and D-dimer, haptoglobin, LDH, reticulocyte count, triglycerides, ferritin, soluble CD25, NK-cell function, CRP and procalcitonin, blood CMV/EBV/HHV-6/HSV/VZV PCR, galactomannan and beta-D-glucan, urinalysis, serum and urine osmolality with urine sodium, cortisol and TSH, and ADAMTS13 if TMA is suspected. Imaging: emergent noncontrast CT head, then MRI brain with and without gadolinium including DWI, SWI and MRV to assess for ICANS, cerebral edema, PRES, venous sinus thrombosis and leptomeningeal disease; MRI can be normal in ICANS and a normal study does not exclude it. Urgent EEG, continuous if available, to exclude nonconvulsive status epilepticus. Lumbar puncture only after imaging and neurosurgical clearance, and after platelets are at least 50,000-100,000/uL and INR is corrected: send cell count, protein, glucose, cytology, flow cytometry, bacterial, fungal and AFB cultures, cryptococcal antigen, HSV/VZV/CMV/EBV/HHV-6/JC PCR, and metagenomic sequencing if available, with opening pressure. Fundoscopy for papilledema, echocardiography if hemodynamically unstable, and bone marrow biopsy only if HLH remains likely after initial testing. Do not delay empiric antibiotics or steroids for these tests; repeat ferritin, CRP, lactate and blood counts to follow the trajectory.

items.criterion: The response recognizes ICANS (ASTCT grade 3: ICE 2/10, GCS 13) and starts corticosteroids (e.g. dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours) promptly.

The response recognizes concurrent CRS (fever with relative hypotension vs baseline, tachycardia, lactate 2.6; grade 1-2 at presentation) and treats it: IV fluid bolus, repeat tocilizumab (dose not exhausted) if hypotension persists, and escalation if refractory; it notes tocilizumab alone does not treat ICANS.

The response treats possible neutropenic sepsis: blood cultures (peripheral and line) and empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g. cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam) within one hour, without waiting for results.
The response addresses airway protection/ICU-level monitoring, frequent neuro checks (ICE/GCS), aspiration and seizure precautions, and continuation/optimization of levetiracetam.
The differential includes CNS relapse of lymphoma, given his high CNS-IPI with kidney/adrenal involvement at diagnosis.
The differential includes CNS infection (bacterial meningitis; HSV/HHV-6 encephalitis) and intracranial hemorrhage (platelets 44).
The differential includes non-convulsive seizures/status and metabolic causes (hyponatremia, hyperglycemia, sepsis-associated encephalopathy, drugs).
The response orders urgent non-contrast CT head (hemorrhage), then MRI brain with contrast.
The response orders an EEG, and a lumbar puncture only once safe (after imaging; platelets transfused to >=50) with CSF cell count, cultures, HSV/HHV-6 PCR, cytology and flow cytometry.
The response anticipates worsening hyperglycemia from dexamethasone in this diabetic patient (glucose 242) and plans insulin adjustment.
The response performs a lumbar puncture immediately, before head imaging or without correcting platelets of 44.
The response withholds corticosteroids for ICANS out of concern that they will harm CAR-T efficacy.
